passages.t: ‘Give me children, or I will die’
passages.happening:
Rachel has no children, and she envies her sister. “Give me children, or I will die!” she says to Jacob (verse 1).

Jacob becomes angry. “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld children from you?” (verse 2).

Rachel says, “Here is my maidservant Bilhah. Sleep with her, that she may bear children for me, so that through her I too can build a family” (verse 3). She gives Bilhah to Jacob as a wife, and Bilhah bears a son (verses 4-5). Rachel says, “God has vindicated me; He has heard my plea and given me a son.” She names him Dan (verse 6).

Bilhah bears a second son. Rachel says, “In my great struggles, I have wrestled with my sister and won.” She names him Naphtali (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Rachel is the loved wife. Leah is the fruitful one. Each has what the other wants. Rachel's cry, ‘Give me children, or I will die’, is the cry of a woman whose whole world told her that a wife without children had failed.

In that world a woman's place in the household, her care in old age, and her husband's family name all depended on children. Childlessness was often felt as shame. Rachel will say so when her son is born: ‘God has taken away my shame’ (verse 23).

Jacob's answer is true and hard. Only God gives life. But he answers his wife's anguish with anger. His grandmother Sarah was barren, and his mother Rebekah too, and his father Isaac prayed for twenty years (25:21). Jacob does not pray. He scolds.

Then Rachel does what Sarah did with Hagar (16:2), using almost the same words: ‘that through her I too can build a family’. Bilhah is an enslaved woman. She is given to Jacob to bear children for her mistress. She has no say in any of it. Her body is used for another woman's plan, as Hagar's was. Genesis calls her a wife, but she stays a servant, and her sons are named by Rachel, not by her.

The names keep score. Dan sounds like ‘vindicated’, ‘judged in my favor’. Naphtali sounds like ‘wrestling’. Rachel says she has wrestled with her sister and won. The sisters are at war, and the children are the weapons.

There is a heavy irony here that the first hearers would feel. Rachel cried that she would die without children. Years later she dies giving birth to her second son (35:16-18).
passages.later:
Hannah's story echoes this one: a loved wife with no children, a rival who taunts her, and a husband who answers, “Am I not better to you than ten sons?” (1 Samuel 1:8). Hannah takes her grief to God in prayer, and he hears her.

Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist, says when she conceives, “He has shown me favor and taken away my disgrace among the people” (Luke 1:25).

Jeremiah later pictures Rachel as the mother of her people, weeping for children who are lost: “Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted” (Jeremiah 31:15). Matthew hears that cry again at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18).
passages.hard:
A word of care. Rachel's story ends with a son. It does not promise a child to every couple who prays for one. Many faithful people long for children and never have them, or lose them before birth. Childlessness is not a judgment from God, and it does not measure your faith. Your longing is seen. If the grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.

Rachel said she would die. Some readers know that feeling, when a longing or a loss makes life itself seem not worth going on with. That feeling is real, and it is heavy, but it is not the last word about your life. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And a word about Bilhah and Zilpah. The Bible does not hide that its great families held slaves and used them. It shows us the harm, so that we can see it. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?’, faces the wider question.
passages.asks: Rachel went to her husband, then to a plan, then to a rival's game. Ask where you take your deepest longing first. Then ask who in your life is paying the cost of a plan you made to get what you want.

passages.happening:
Leah sees that she has stopped having children. So she gives her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife (verse 9).

Zilpah bears Jacob a son. Leah says, “How fortunate!” and names him Gad (verses 10-11).

Zilpah bears a second son. Leah says, “How happy I am! For the women call me happy.” She names him Asher (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
Now Leah does the same as her sister. The contest spreads.

Zilpah, too, is an enslaved woman. She is given to Jacob to bear children for Leah. She has no say. Her sons are counted as Leah's and named by Leah. The text does not tell us a single word that Zilpah or Bilhah said. Their silence in the story is part of what the story shows.

Gad means ‘good fortune’. Asher means ‘happy’. Leah's earlier names were about her husband's love and her praise to God. These two are about luck and what other women say. She is playing the game now too.

Yet each of these sons will become the father of a tribe of Israel. The children of the enslaved women are full members of God's people, with their own land and their own blessing (49:16-21). They are not second-class sons.
passages.later:
Jacob blesses all twelve sons before he dies, the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah with the rest: “These are the tribes of Israel, twelve in all” (Genesis 49:28).

Revelation writes the names of the twelve tribes on the gates of the city of God: “twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel” (Revelation 21:12). The sons of Bilhah and Zilpah are written there with the sons of Leah and Rachel.

Israel's law later set limits on how a servant woman taken as a wife could be treated. She could not be sold to foreigners, and if she was denied food, clothing or marital rights, she went free (Exodus 21:7-11).
passages.asks: Bilhah and Zilpah are never heard in their own words. Ask whose voices go unheard in your family, your church or your work. Then ask what it would take to hear them.

passages.happening:
At the wheat harvest, Reuben finds mandrakes in a field and brings them to his mother Leah. Rachel asks, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes” (verse 14).

Leah answers, “Is it not enough that you have taken away my husband? Now you want to take my son’s mandrakes as well?” Rachel says, “he may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes” (verse 15).

That evening Leah meets Jacob: “You must come with me, for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes” (verse 16).

“And God listened to Leah”, and she bears a fifth son, Issachar (verses 17-18). Then a sixth, Zebulun: “This time my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons” (verse 20). After that she has a daughter, Dinah (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Mandrakes are a low plant with a thick root and small, sweet-smelling yellow fruit that ripens in late spring. People in the ancient world believed they stirred up love and helped a woman to conceive. Their Hebrew name sounds like a word for love. That is why Rachel wants them. The plant is in fact poisonous if too much is eaten, and there is no good evidence that it helps anyone have a child.

Leah's answer is full of pain: ‘Is it not enough that you have taken away my husband?’ The sisters are trading their husband's nights like goods at a market. Jacob is hired for a handful of plants.

Then the twist. Rachel gets the mandrakes, and Leah gets pregnant. The text gives the reason plainly: ‘God listened to Leah’. Whatever the mandrakes were believed to do, the writer does not credit them with anything.

Issachar sounds like ‘wages’ or ‘hire’. Zebulun sounds like ‘honor’ and ‘gift’. And still Leah hopes: ‘This time my husband will honor me.’

Dinah is the only daughter named. Her name is not explained. Her story comes in chapter 34.
passages.later:
The Song of Songs mentions the same plant as part of love's delights: “The mandrakes send forth a fragrance” (Song of Songs 7:13).

God listening to a woman in her longing runs through the Bible. Hannah prayed, and “the LORD remembered her” (1 Samuel 1:19).
passages.asks: The sisters fought over a plant that could not give what only God gives. Ask what you are trusting to give you what only God can give. Then notice that God listened to Leah, the one who had less.

passages.happening:
“Then God remembered Rachel. He listened to her and opened her womb” (verse 22).

She bears a son. “God has taken away my shame,” she says (verse 23). She names him Joseph, and says, “May the LORD add to me another son” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
‘God remembered’ does not mean God had forgotten. In the Bible, when God remembers someone, he acts for them. God remembered Noah in the flood (8:1). Now he remembers Rachel.

And ‘He listened to her’ tells us she had been praying. Her prayer is not written down. But after the anger, the plan with Bilhah and the mandrakes, the child comes as God's answer, not as the prize of a contest.

Joseph's name plays on two words. It sounds like ‘he has taken away’ (my shame) and like ‘may he add’ (another son). In the moment of joy she is already longing for more.

This is the son the rest of Genesis is about. Joseph, the son of the loved wife, will be hated by his brothers, sold into Egypt, and used by God to save them all.
passages.later:
God remembers in the same way when he hears Israel in Egypt: “God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Exodus 2:24).

A psalm praises God who “settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children” (Psalm 113:9).

Stephen tells Joseph's story to the council in Jerusalem, of a brother rejected and then the one through whom God saved his family (Acts 7:9-14).
passages.asks: Rachel's son came after years of struggle, as a gift from God who listened. Ask what you have been waiting for. Then ask whether you can trust that God hears you, even before you see the answer.

passages.happening:
After Joseph is born, Jacob asks Laban to let him go home with his wives and children (verses 25-26).

Laban says, “please stay. I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you” (verse 27). “Name your wages, and I will pay them” (verse 28).

Jacob reminds him: “you had very little before my arrival, but now your wealth has increased many times over. The LORD has blessed you wherever I set foot” (verse 30). He asks for no payment now. Instead, he will take as his wages every speckled or spotted sheep and goat, and every dark-colored lamb, born from now on (verses 31-33).

“Agreed,” says Laban (verse 34). That very day Laban removes every streaked, spotted and dark animal from the flock, gives them to his sons, and puts “a three-day journey” between them and Jacob (verses 35-36).
passages.hearers:
Fourteen years have passed. Jacob has paid for both his wives with his work. Now he wants to go home.

Laban admits something remarkable. He has found out ‘by divination’ that the LORD has blessed him because of Jacob. Divination means trying to learn hidden things by signs or omens. Israel's law later forbade it (Deuteronomy 18:10). Laban worships other gods (as the next chapter shows), but he can see the LORD's blessing on Jacob. God promised Abraham, ‘through you all the families of the earth will be blessed’ (12:3). Here even a cheat is blessed through Jacob.

Jacob's offer looks modest. Commentators have long noted that in that region sheep were usually white and goats usually dark, so speckled and spotted animals were few. Jacob asks only for the odd ones.

Then Laban shows who he is. He says ‘Agreed’, and that same day he takes away every animal that could give Jacob a start. He sends them three days' travel away. Jacob is left with only plain-colored animals, and a promise that he may keep whatever odd ones are born.

Laban's name means ‘white’. Keep that in mind for the next part.
passages.later:
Jacob later says Laban “cheated me and changed my wages ten times” (Genesis 31:7).

Israel's law later protected hired workers: “You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand” (Leviticus 19:13). James warns those who cheat workers of their pay (James 5:4).
passages.asks: Laban saw God's blessing on Jacob and still tried to cheat him. Ask whether you have ever benefited from someone and then tried to keep them small. Then ask how you treat the people whose work makes your life better.

passages.happening:
Jacob takes fresh branches of poplar, almond and plane trees, and peels the bark to show “the white inner wood” (verse 37). He sets the peeled branches in the watering troughs where the flocks come to drink and to mate (verse 38). The animals mate in front of the branches, “And they bore young that were streaked or speckled or spotted” (verse 39).

Jacob keeps his own animals apart from Laban's (verse 40). He sets out the branches only when the stronger animals are mating, not the weaker ones. “So the weaker animals went to Laban and the stronger ones to Jacob” (verses 41-42).

“Thus Jacob became exceedingly prosperous” (verse 43), with large flocks, servants, camels and donkeys.
passages.hearers:
Jacob seems to have believed, as many people in the ancient world did, that what an animal saw while mating would mark its young. That was a folk practice. The text reports what Jacob did. It does not say the branches worked.

In fact, the next chapter gives a different account. Jacob tells his wives that in a dream the angel of God showed him which males were mating with the flock, and said, ‘I have seen all that Laban has done to you’ (31:10-12). Jacob says plainly, ‘God has taken away your father's livestock and given them to me’ (31:9). By Jacob's own later word, the increase came from God, not from the sticks.

There is a pun here that the first hearers would enjoy. Laban's name means ‘white’. Jacob beats ‘White’ by peeling branches down to the white wood. Even the Hebrew word for poplar sounds like Laban's name.

Is Jacob cheating? Readers differ. Some see sharp practice answering sharp practice: Laban cheated first, and Jacob outwits him. Others think Jacob kept to the deal Laban himself accepted, and only chose which animals to breed. The text lets both men be shrewd. It does not hold Jacob up as a model. It shows God keeping his promise to bless Jacob, in a crooked situation, through a flawed man.
passages.later:
Jacob's own account is in the next chapter: “Thus God has taken away your father’s livestock and given them to me” (Genesis 31:9), and the angel says, “I have seen all that Laban has done to you” (Genesis 31:12).

God had promised at Bethel, “I will watch over you wherever you go” (Genesis 28:15). Proverbs says, “The blessing of the LORD enriches, and He adds no sorrow to it” (Proverbs 10:22).
passages.asks: Jacob worked his methods, and God gave the increase. Ask what you are relying on your own cleverness to get. Then ask whether you would give God the credit, as Jacob finally did, if it came.
